lessons.title: Semantic HTML for Application Interfaces
lessons.summary: HTML describes document/interface structure and meaning, not visual styling.
lessons.body:
Semantic HTML for Application Interfaces

Why this matters
HTML describes document/interface structure and meaning, not visual styling. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• HTML describes document/interface structure and meaning, not visual styling.
• Use headings in order, buttons for actions, anchors for navigation, labels for form controls, lists for collections, and landmarks for page regions.
• Semantic elements provide keyboard and assistive-technology behavior you would otherwise need to recreate.
• A React component still renders HTML; framework code does not cancel platform semantics.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, html, css, accessibility, and responsive layout stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter semantic html for application interfaces again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: CSS Cascade, Box Model, and Specificity
lessons.summary: Every element participates in layout with content, padding, border, and margin.
lessons.body:

Why this matters

lessons.title: Layout with Normal Flow, Flexbox, and Grid
lessons.summary: Normal document flow should remain the default until a layout requirement earns another model.
lessons.body:
Layout with Normal Flow, Flexbox, and Grid

Why this matters
Normal document flow should remain the default until a layout requirement earns another model. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Normal document flow should remain the default until a layout requirement earns another model.
• Flexbox is strongest for one-dimensional alignment/distribution; Grid is strongest for two-dimensional tracks.
• Absolute positioning removes an element from normal flow and should be used for overlays/badges rather than entire application layout by habit.
• min-width, overflow, and intrinsic content often explain layouts that 'refuse to shrink'.

lessons.title: Responsive Design and Container Thinking
lessons.summary: Responsive design is not a pile of device-specific pixel values; it is content adapting as available space changes.
lessons.body:
Responsive Design and Container Thinking

Why this matters
Responsive design is not a pile of device-specific pixel values; it is content adapting as available space changes. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Responsive design is not a pile of device-specific pixel values; it is content adapting as available space changes.
• Prefer fluid sizes and component/container constraints, then add breakpoints where the design actually breaks.
• Test keyboard, zoom, long labels, empty states, and narrow widths—not just a perfect desktop screenshot.
• An iframe/component may see a different viewport/container than the host page, so choose media/container queries intentionally.

lessons.title: Accessibility as Engineering Correctness
lessons.summary: Keyboard access, focus visibility, labels, headings, contrast, and reduced-motion behavior are functional requirements.
lessons.body:
Accessibility as Engineering Correctness

Why this matters
Keyboard access, focus visibility, labels, headings, contrast, and reduced-motion behavior are functional requirements. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Keyboard access, focus visibility, labels, headings, contrast, and reduced-motion behavior are functional requirements.
• ARIA can expose semantics when native elements cannot, but incorrect ARIA can make interfaces worse.
• Error messages should identify the field/problem and remain programmatically associated with the control.
• Automated checks help, but manual keyboard and screen-reader-oriented reasoning still matter.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, html, css, accessibility, and responsive layout stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter accessibility as engineering correctness again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Lab — Accessibility as Engineering Correctness
lessons.summary: Hands-on transfer lab for the preceding concept.
lessons.body:
Lab: Accessibility as Engineering Correctness

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Build the smallest runnable example for “Accessibility as Engineering Correctness”, predict its output, change one assumption, and explain the difference using concrete evidence.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.

Compare prediction with actual runtime evidence.
Diagnose one intentionally introduced failure.
